passages.original: Tacendum esse non credo quod, cum de Aegypto loquor, vetus suggessit historia, simul etiam Gallieni factum, qui cum Theodoto vellet imperium proconsulare decernere, a sacerdotibus est prohibitus, qui dixerunt fasces consulares ingredi Alexandriam non licere, cuius rei etiam Ciceronem, cum contra Gabinium loquitur, meminisse satis novimus, denique nunc exstat memoria rei frequentatae. quare scire oportet Herennium Celsum, vestrum parentem, cum consulatum cupit, hoc quod desiderat non licere. fertur enim apud Memphim in aurea columna Aegyptiis esse litteris scriptum tunc demum Aegyptum liberam fore cum in eam venissent Romani fasces et praetexta Romanorum, quod apud Proculum grammaticum, doctissimum sui temporis virum, cum de peregrinis regionibus loquitur, invenitur.
passages.english: I do not think I should pass over in silence what ancient history suggests, since I am speaking of Egypt, and at the same time an act of Gallienus: when he wished to decree proconsular command to Theodotus, he was prevented by the priests, who said that it was not lawful for the consular fasces to enter Alexandria. We know well enough that Cicero too mentions this matter when he speaks against Gabinius, and indeed the memory of the matter, often repeated, survives even now. Therefore Herennius Celsus, your kinsman, should know, since he desires the consulship, that what he longs for is not lawful. For it is said that at Memphis, on a golden column, it was written in Egyptian letters that Egypt would only then be free when the Roman fasces and the bordered toga of the Romans had come into it. This is found in Proculus the grammarian, the most learned man of his time, where he speaks of foreign regions.
passages.notes: "vestrum parentem": parens here likely means 'kinsman' or 'relative' rather than literally 'father'; the addressee (plural 'your') is unclear. "imperium proconsulare" = proconsular command. "praetexta" = the toga praetexta, the purple-bordered toga of Roman magistrates.
